title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
Data sheet: primary website query



Terms: Trump, Kamala Harris, Election (each selected as a search term, not a topic)
Geography: United States (US) · Window: past five years (today+5-y)
Category: all (0) · Search type: Web Search (web)
Pulled: 2026-09-12 16:38:24 CDT
Query: Google Trends Explore
The website CSV covers 2021-09-12 through 2026-09-06 at weekly intervals. With the same three terms but a 90-day window, the CSV covers 2026-06-12 through 2026-09-12 daily. Thus, Google changed the time resolution with the window. My additional current-news term was Federal Reserve (US, past 90 days, all categories, Web Search), pulled 2026-09-12 16:39:35 CDT; the term was timely because an FOMC meeting was scheduled for September 15–16 (Federal Reserve calendar).

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
R pull and comparison


Code
library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

r_pull <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Kamala Harris", "Election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE, geo = "US", gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y", category = 0
)
write_csv(r_pull$interest_over_time,
          "data/r_trump_kamala-election_us_5y_2026-09-12.csv")




Code
ggplot(web, aes(date, hits, color = keyword)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = r |> group_by(keyword) |> slice(seq(1, n(), by = 13)),
             shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 1.7, stroke = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~keyword, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2A9D8F", "#6C5CE7", "#E76F51")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Google Trends index (0–100)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())





Figure 1: Weekly Google search-interest index. Lines are the website CSV; open points are every thirteenth gtrendsR observation. Exact overlap means the two pulls matched in this run.




After mapping the website’s <1 cells to zero, all 783 aligned observations were identical: mean absolute difference 0, maximum difference 0, and therefore no direction of difference. The raw files are still structurally different: the website is wide, uses Week and <1, and puts the category in a preamble; R is long and adds query metadata to every row. This is a result of these particular pulls, not a guarantee.
Google Trends is not a count. Google says it samples searches, divides each point by total searches for its time and geography, and rescales within the query from 0 to 100. Thus 100 is the query’s peak relative interest; 0 generally means too little volume to report, not necessarily no searches. Google also cautions that Trends is not polling and that a spike does not mean a topic is “winning” (Google Trends FAQ).

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
Sensitivity and method choice
Removing Kamala Harris and rerunning the five-year website query changed 67 of 522 remaining observations (12.8%). Every changed cell rose in the two-term pull; the largest increase was four index points. This happens because the sample and the within-query normalization are recomputed, so values are comparable only inside the query that produced them.
Harris and Kamala Harris were not the same series: in a joint R query none of their 261 weekly values matched; the mean absolute gap was 7.46 and the maximum was 35 index points. A search term measures the literal words entered, whereas a Google Trends topic groups searches for a concept across wording and languages (Google’s term-versus-topic guide). The bare surname therefore does not isolate the intended person.
The website is transparent to inspect but manual: its interest-over-time CSV records the category plus term/geography labels, while my separate query log had to preserve the time window, search type, term-versus-topic choice, and pull time. The R output records keyword, geo, time, gprop, and category in every row and scales to many scripted terms, countries, and repetitions. Neither route guarantees identical future values, but R makes the procedure far easier to regenerate. It is also fragile: gtrendsR depends on an unofficial endpoint, so rate limits or a changed response can break a call; my first website load returned HTTP 429 before a retry succeeded. I cache the first success, retain the raw RDS/CSV, and check row counts, date ranges, and missing values.
With onlyInterest = FALSE, names(tct) returned interest_over_time plus interest_by_country, interest_by_region, interest_by_dma, interest_by_city, related_topics, and related_queries. The single website chart download contained only the first; the other six were absent. The package documents these list-based results and the onlyInterest switch (gtrendsR reference manual).
I also completed and cached the required extensions: Taylor Swift over time = "all", the same term in Great Britain, the term across c("US", "GB", "TW"), and Taylor Swift, Beyonce, and Adele worldwide.
Finally, two identical Federal Reserve R calls returned the same 93 daily values in this run. Because Google describes Trends as sampled data with small statistical noise, equality once does not establish stability. Any reported finding should archive its exact pull, be checked with repetitions, and avoid overinterpreting small differences (Google Trends FAQ).
The complete cached workflow is in code/gtrendsR01.R; derived comparisons are produced by code/analyze_trends.R.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
For this assignment, I use the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates to look at how income and poverty vary across Texas counties. I map median household income and rank counties by poverty rate. I use a rate instead of the number of people below poverty because a count would mostly reflect differences in county population size.






Geography and variables




Geography: Texas counties
Median household income: B19013_001
Population below poverty: B17001_002
Population for whom poverty status was determined: B17001_001
Survey: 2024 ACS five-year estimates (acs5)



The Census API key was installed once in .Renviron; it is not stored in this document or in the public repository.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Variable metadata and data retrieval
I first check the variable codes against the 2024 ACS five-year metadata. The current tidycensus interface loads the metadata directly from the Census API, so I do not use the deprecated cache argument.


Code
vars <- load_variables(2024, "acs5")

vars |>
  filter(name %in% c("B19013_001", "B17001_001", "B17001_002")) |>
  select(name, label, concept) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Variable", "Label", "Concept"),
    align = c("l", "l", "l")
  )




Table 1: ACS variables used in the analysis.







Variable
Label
Concept




B17001_001
Estimate!!Total:
Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age


B17001_002
Estimate!!Total:!!Income in the past 12 months below poverty level:
Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age


B19013_001
Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months (in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars)
Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months (in 2024 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars)






The next call downloads the estimates, margins of error, and county geometry in wide form. In the resulting column names, E identifies an estimate and M identifies its margin of error.


Code
state_abbr <- "TX"
geo_level <- "county"
year_acs <- 2024
survey_name <- "acs5"

my_vars <- c(
  income = "B19013_001",
  pov = "B17001_002",
  povden = "B17001_001"
)

acs_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = geo_level,
  variables = my_vars,
  state = state_abbr,
  year = year_acs,
  survey = survey_name,
  geometry = TRUE,
  output = "wide"
)

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
section: Constructing the poverty rate and uncertainty interval
text:
Constructing the poverty rate and uncertainty interval
I calculate the poverty rate by dividing the estimated number of people below poverty by the estimated population for whom poverty status was determined. Because both values come from a sample, I carry their uncertainty into the rate with moe_prop(). ACS margins of error are reported at the 90% confidence level, so I construct each interval as the estimate plus or minus its MOE.


Code
acs_wide <- acs_wide |>
  mutate(
    pov_rate = povE / povdenE,
    pov_rate_moe = moe_prop(povE, povdenE, povM, povdenM),
    pov_ci_low = pmax(0, pov_rate - pov_rate_moe),
    pov_ci_high = pmin(1, pov_rate + pov_rate_moe)
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(acs_wide) == 254,
  !anyNA(acs_wide$incomeE),
  !anyNA(acs_wide$pov_rate),
  all(acs_wide$povdenE > 0)
)

write_csv(
  st_drop_geometry(acs_wide),
  "data/acs_TX_county_2024.csv"
)

Median household income map


Code
ggplot(acs_wide) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = incomeE), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    name = "Median household\nincome (2024 $)",
    labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1, big.mark = ",")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Household Income by County in Texas",
    subtitle = "ACS 2024 five-year estimates",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau via tidycensus."
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "right"
  )





Figure 1: Median household income across Texas counties. Values are ACS 2024 five-year estimates.




Estimated median household income ranges from $36,165 to $127,981. Rockwall and Collin counties are at the high end of the distribution. Swisher, Zavala, Starr, Dimmit, and Zapata counties are among those at the low end. This map shows where the estimates are higher or lower, but it does not explain what caused those differences.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Poverty-rate ranking
Before ranking the counties, I remove the geometry and keep the full-precision values for all calculations. I round only the numbers displayed in the table. The poverty-rate estimate and its MOE are both reported in percentage points.


Code
poverty_data <- acs_wide |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(pov_rate), !is.na(pov_rate_moe), povdenE > 0)

top10 <- poverty_data |>
  arrange(desc(pov_rate)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(group = "Highest 10")

bottom10 <- poverty_data |>
  arrange(pov_rate) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(group = "Lowest 10")

ranked_table <- bind_rows(top10, bottom10) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()

table_for_display <- ranked_table |>
  transmute(
    Group = group,
    Rank = rank,
    County = sub(", Texas$", "", NAME),
    `Poverty rate` = scales::percent(pov_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    `MOE` = scales::percent(pov_rate_moe, accuracy = 0.1),
    `90% confidence interval` = paste0(
      scales::percent(pov_ci_low, accuracy = 0.1),
      " to ",
      scales::percent(pov_ci_high, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  table_for_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Group", "Rank", "County", "Poverty rate",
    "MOE", "90% confidence interval"
  ),
  align = c("l", "r", "l", "r", "r", "r")
)

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Uncertainty check


Code
overlap_example <- ranked_table |>
  filter(NAME %in% c("Dimmit County, Texas", "Zapata County, Texas")) |>
  transmute(
    County = sub(", Texas$", "", NAME),
    Estimate = scales::percent(pov_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    MOE = scales::percent(pov_rate_moe, accuracy = 0.1),
    `90% confidence interval` = paste0(
      scales::percent(pov_ci_low, accuracy = 0.1),
      " to ",
      scales::percent(pov_ci_high, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(overlap_example, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))

Dimmit County’s 90% confidence interval is 32.2% to 50.0%, and Zapata County’s is 32.4% to 44.4%. These intervals overlap substantially. Dimmit ranks above Zapata when I use the point estimates, but the ACS sampling uncertainty means that I cannot confidently conclude that Dimmit’s underlying poverty rate is higher. I therefore treat the table as a ranking of estimates rather than a precise ordering of the counties’ true rates.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Methods note
For this project, I use the 2024 ACS five-year estimates for all 254 Texas counties. I map median household income (B19013_001) and calculate poverty rates by dividing the estimated population below poverty (B17001_002) by the population for whom poverty status was determined (B17001_001). This rate is more useful for comparing counties than a count, which is strongly affected by population size. I use moe_prop() to carry the numerator and denominator margins of error into the poverty rate, and I report 90% confidence intervals. Dimmit and Zapata counties rank first and second by their point estimates, but their intervals overlap. This overlap means that the data do not clearly establish which county has the higher underlying poverty rate. I therefore interpret the table as a descriptive ranking rather than an exact ordering. Data were retrieved from the U.S. Census Bureau through tidycensus.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Reproducibility
The analysis retrieves the estimates and geometry from the Census API. I also save a geometry-free copy of the complete dataset as data/acs_TX_county_2024.csv. The CSV includes the original estimates and MOEs, the derived poverty rate and its propagated MOE, and the lower and upper limits of the 90% confidence interval.

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping and Data Acquisition
text:
Warm-up: Books to Scrape
I first used Books to Scrape, a sandbox intended for scraping practice. Each page has 20 article.product_pod cards. I extracted the title attribute, the displayed price, and the rating class, paused between requests, and bound pages 1–5 into one dataframe.


Code
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(rvest)
library(stringr)
library(tibble)

rating_levels <- c(One = 1L, Two = 2L, Three = 3L, Four = 4L, Five = 5L)

scrape_books_page <- function(page_number) {
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
  cards <- read_html(sprintf(
    "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-%s.html", page_number
  )) |>
    html_elements("article.product_pod")

  tibble(
    page = page_number,
    title = cards |> html_element("h3 a") |> html_attr("title"),
    price_gbp = cards |>
      html_element("p.price_color") |>
      html_text2() |>
      parse_number(),
    rating_word = cards |>
      html_element("p.star-rating") |>
      html_attr("class") |>
      str_remove("^star-rating\\s+")
  ) |>
    mutate(rating = unname(rating_levels[rating_word]))
}

books <- map_dfr(1:5, scrape_books_page)
stopifnot(nrow(books) == 100L, !anyDuplicated(books$title))

Vintage explains part of the disagreement, but not all of it: even same-year records can differ sharply. Wikipedia combines volunteer-edited figures from many national sources and uses irregular observation dates; the World Bank indicator is a harmonized annual series with its own coverage and valuation conventions. Country naming and revisions add further differences, and extreme examples such as North Macedonia show why the scraped table should not be treated as an authoritative statistical series. The relevant comparison is therefore source provenance and definition, not merely whether two formatted numbers look close.
Scraping is appropriate when the needed public information has no usable API, bulk download, or structured file and the site’s rules permit automated access. When an official API supplies the same quantity with stable identifiers and metadata, I would use the API and reserve scraping for validation or fields the API omits.

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping and Data Acquisition
section: Data plan: gambling availability and local harm
text:
Data plan: gambling availability and local harm
My research examines how gambling availability and vice-market regulation shape crime and behavioral harm. I would build a county-by-month record of licensed gambling venues, openings, closings, operator changes, and enforcement actions. The primary sources would be state gaming commission license registries and disciplinary-order pages because they are the legal record of market access. Commercial directories are easier to search but can be stale, omit closures, or mix licensed and unlicensed businesses. I would cross-check addresses and business names against state business registries and geocode only after preserving the original agency text.
Before collection, I would archive the URL, collection date, robots.txt response, and the relevant Terms of Service for each state. Permission would be evaluated at the exact paths I intend to request, not inferred from the home page. A disallowed path, login requirement, CAPTCHA, or anti-automation clause would stop automated collection. Public availability alone is not permission to create an aggressive crawler.
I would first look for an API, open-data portal, downloadable CSV, or periodic bulk file. If one exists, I would use it because stable identifiers and documented fields are more valuable than copying an HTML view. Scraping would be justified only for states that publish required events solely as public HTML tables or order-detail pages. PDFs would be downloaded as source documents when permitted, with extraction treated separately because a PDF’s visible layout is not a database schema.
The expected volume is modest: dozens of state index pages and a few thousand detail records per annual refresh. Each host would have its own queue with a descriptive user agent, one request at a time, a delay of at least one second, exponential backoff for 429 or 5xx responses, and no repeated request for an unchanged URL. Raw responses would be cached by retrieval date and content hash. A manifest would record URL, status, timestamp, content type, byte size, checksum, parser version, and any retry. Derived tables would never replace the raw snapshot.
Page changes can break a CSS selector without producing an obvious error. I would test expected columns, plausible row counts, unique license IDs, parse success for dates and coordinates, and the fraction of missing addresses. A daily or weekly run would compare these diagnostics with the previous snapshot and quarantine a result when the table count changes, a required column disappears, or missingness jumps. I would manually inspect a sample of additions, deletions, and changed addresses before publishing an update. This design makes a layout change visible as a failed validation rather than a silent change in the research dataset.
The complete collection and validation workflow is in code/assignment04_collect.R. Clean data and the robots check are stored under data/assignment04/.

text:
What Wordfish measures


Code
wordfish |>
  left_join(inaugural |> select(document, year, party), by = "document") |>
  ggplot(aes(wordfish_position, reorder(document, wordfish_position), color = party)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    Democratic = "#2E86AB",
    Republican = "#D1495B"
  )) +
  labs(x = "Estimated Wordfish position", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())





Figure 4: Wordfish document positions for inaugural addresses. Orientation is fixed from Roosevelt 1945 toward Reagan 1981.




Wordfish treats each document-feature count as a Poisson outcome. A word has an overall frequency and a discrimination parameter, while each document has a latent position and a document-level size parameter. The fitted dimension is whatever single contrast best explains systematic differences in word use; it is not inherently left-right ideology. In these speeches it may combine period, rhetorical style, war and peace, economic conditions, and party. Establishing a substantive meaning would require external validation, sensitivity to preprocessing and document selection, and close reading of words with strong discrimination parameters. The sign is unidentified, so dir anchors the orientation; without it, an equivalent fit could be reflected left-to-right.

text:
Comparison and data note
The tweets are user-produced messages selected by a platform query and an event window; they can support claims about the collected conversation, not all citizens. The presidential documents are institutionally produced and support claims about official rhetoric, not private policy preferences or public reaction. The inaugural addresses are ceremonial texts selected by political tradition and are useful for long-run rhetorical comparison, but their changing historical context limits causal interpretation.

These YouTube comments were produced by a self-selected audience under videos chosen by publishers and ranked by YouTube. They support claims about the comments the API returned, not voters or the general public.

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Question and data note



The linked file is intended to estimate how many simulated people appear in both the Teacher Retirement System (TRS) and Texas Education Agency (TEA) files. Both files contain 500 fictional records, the complete answer key contains 100 true pairs, and set.seed(42) is retained. I publish aggregate results and fictional record IDs, not the generated names or dates of birth.

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Model and assumptions
The Fellegi-Sunter model estimates how likely each field agreement is among true matches (m) and non-matches (u), then combines the evidence into a match weight or probability under explicit assumptions. The workshop’s weighted score instead assigns fixed importance to three similarities and is not a calibrated probability.
A reliable unique identifier can be joined deterministically because agreement carries much stronger identifying information than a common name or birth date. Records without such an identifier require probabilistic evidence and uncertainty; even an ID should be audited when entry errors, reuse, or missingness are possible.
My deterministic stage applies the workshop’s three sequential rules: exact standardized full name and DOB; standardized last name, first initial, and DOB; and exact full name with DOB within one day. It removes linked records after each rule. The probabilistic stage uses Jaro-Winkler similarities for both names and an exact/one-day DOB score, blocks on the first letter of standardized last name, and greedily retains one-to-one pairs from highest to lowest score.

I removed the workshop line that sliced the validation data to its first 100 rows. The maximum movement of precision, recall, or F1 across the threshold curve was 0.0%. In a real evaluation, an arbitrary prefix could overrepresent easy cases, exclude later sources or groups, and bias every reported metric.

I choose 0.97, the highest threshold attaining the maximum observed F1. Wrongly joining two people’s administrative records can expose or attribute information to the wrong person, so I prioritize precision and choose the most conservative threshold that does not reduce measured recall. A reviewer should reject that case on this answer key, although one simulated case is too small to estimate review accuracy.

title: Assignment 8: Record Linkage
text:
Limits
This linked file demonstrates a method, not the reliability of a real TRS-TEA linkage. The answer key is generated and complete, names come from short lists, corruption affects one field at a time, and there are no missing values, households, aliases, duplicate people, or group-specific error rates. Real data would need secure handling, a defensible validation sample, clerical review, sensitivity to alternative blocks and thresholds, and fairness checks by name frequency and data quality. Without a trustworthy answer key, reported precision and recall become estimates whose credibility depends on how validation cases were selected.
The reproducible workflow is in code/assignment08_linkage.R, and the data-generating process, rules, weights, threshold, review band, and known gaps are recorded in data/assignment08/assignment08_manifest.json.
AI-use disclosure: I used an AI coding assistant to help adapt the instructor’s workshop, implement diagnostics, and structure the report. I checked the generated data, linkage rules, metrics, and every reported output before submission.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data API
text:
Usability as data
The PDFs are readable records but awkward data. They mix front matter, committee rosters, prepared statements, testimony, question-and-answer exchanges, appendices, and page furniture. A ten-document corpus would require text extraction or OCR, removal of repeated headers and page numbers, speaker segmentation, document-level metadata, and checks against the visible PDF. Tables and scanned exhibits would need separate treatment, and a failed text layer could silently turn a long hearing into an almost empty document.
The process improves immediately by using the alternative formats already named in each API result. HTML or text is easier to tokenize than PDF, MODS supplies structured bibliographic metadata, and the summary endpoint identifies committee, witnesses, dates, and stable package IDs without opening the file. I would cache the raw response, preserve the package ID as the primary key, prefer HTML for the corpus, and use the PDF only to verify layout-dependent material.
The API gave me stable identifiers, structured metadata, explicit download links, and a paging token that can be recorded and rerun. The search page was useful for discovery and last week’s scraper copied a changing table, but neither exposed the same machine-readable contract for retrieving and joining documents.
The complete workflow is in code/assignment05_collect.R. It validates row counts, caches successful results, logs every download, and keeps the documents outside the published repository.
